attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, not a quotation.

semantics.note: 'Which' points back to AI being unable to do many expert tasks. Reading that as AI limitations being a contributing cause of rehiring is faithful, and 'part of why' is kept.

contract.note: Treating the cause as contributing rather than sole, and counting refilled roles as rehiring, is an ordinary and fair reading. The lookback period is unspecified but limited to decisions made by the post date.

evidence.note: A multi-company employer survey from Feb 2026 reports eliminated roles were refilled, and many respondents cite more human oversight than expected. The aggregate figures do not tie each rehire to a cause.

WSJ report of 27 July 2026: a named CEO says employers recalibrated after finding AI agents could not replace the work, and the article reports AI limitations prompting more hiring. Partly about lifting hiring freezes, not only rehiring.
A 2025 case where CBA reversed planned AI redundancies. That is a cancelled cut, not completed rehiring, and it falls outside the main period.
Secondary account of Klarna disputing the AI-quality reading, so Klarna cannot serve as an example. It does not refute the multi-company claim.

reviews.rationale: The survey shows roles being refilled after AI-led layoffs, with unmet automation and oversight needs cited. The WSJ report gives a named executive's account of AI limitations driving renewed hiring. That meets the support condition for a contributing cause across several companies. The Klarna dispute and the CBA reversal are context and do not refute it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own count, stated in his post.

semantics.note: An observation of current capability, with the 'by my count' qualifier kept. The ten tasks come from the Marcus–Brundage bet.

contract.note: Scoring the objective count against the bet's original task standards is fair. Support requires evidence capping the total at two; contradiction requires three established passes.

evidence.note: The original bet text. It defines the tasks and judging rules but is not evidence of capability.
SIMA 2 preprint showing progress on generalising to unfamiliar game worlds. It does not meet the bet's game criterion.
Large-scale autoformalisation in topology before the post. It is not the bet's cross-field proof test.

reviews.rationale: No task-by-task scorecard for July 2026 exists in the packet. The evidence shows partial progress on the game and formalisation tasks, but establishes neither three passes nor an upper bound of two. The packet does not settle the count.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. The WSJ quotation that follows is separate from this claim.

semantics.note: The checkable core is the observation that the boast-then-rehire pattern is happening again. The singularity inference is rhetorical framing and is reasonably assessed separately.

contract.note: The 'Klarna Effect' describes the same employers touting AI cuts and then rehiring, so requiring that link is fair. A July 2026 window follows from 'once again' and the late-July report.

evidence.note: WSJ report via Mint: renewed hiring, with some executives wanting to rehire after layoffs. It does not identify employers that had touted AI-driven cuts.
LinkedIn summary saying laid-off staff are being brought back because of AI's drawbacks. It merely restates the WSJ report and does not document any prior AI boasts.

reviews.rationale: There is some support for rehiring after layoffs that cites AI's drawbacks. But no source in the packet shows the same employers first publicising AI-driven cuts and then restoring human roles in July 2026. Nothing contradicts the claim either, so the evidence does not settle it.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. Diamandis and Musk appear only as the targets of his claim.

semantics.note: An unhedged statement that the age of abundance had not arrived by the post date.

contract.note: Reading 'abundance' as broad material plenty with broad affordability gains is the ordinary sense. Using June 2026 as the latest data period is reasonable.

evidence.note: Official BLS figures for June 2026: US CPI up 3.5% year on year, so no broad fall in prices.
FAO-WFP report of June 2026: about 266 million people face high acute food insecurity. That is inconsistent with widespread access to essentials.
Reuters: a one-month CPI fall of 0.4%, driven mainly by energy. An isolated drop, not a sign of abundance.

reviews.rationale: Prices kept rising year on year, and large populations faced acute food insecurity around June 2026. That meets the support condition of substantial deprivation with no broad affordability transformation. The single monthly CPI drop does not change this.
